gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker Nano 6-in-1's 67 W USB-C figure only applies when it is the only port in use: Anker's own port table cuts it to 45 W once one USB-A device is plugged in, and to 45 W + 20 W with two USB-C devices. So a 65 W laptop charging next to a phone gets 45 W, not the 67 W shown on ChatGPT's 'Fast charging · up to 67W' card.
standout_why: I read four pages ChatGPT got. Tom's Guide was the only one it cited, and WebFetch returned that page truncated, so I could not check its text. rottenwifi.com already says the Anker 351 gives 20 W on USB-C only when its USB-A ports are idle, and that CyberPower's P405UC has 18 W total, so the 351 sharing point is taken. itechguides.com explains shared output only for the Nano Clamp 70W, Prime 240W, Baseus and Belkin, never mentions the 67 W Nano station or its 45 W split, and doesn't mention TESSAN. inspectandtest.net makes the general point that no listing states a UL 1449 VPR and that joule figures are what each seller claims, so that part is partly taken. It doesn't give a per-port USB-C split for any product, and it says nothing about AC load ceilings. None of the four gives the TESSAN PS07's 1,250 W AC limit against 1,875 W on the Anker strips.
decides: If you put every product on the same footing ('laptop on USB-C while a phone charges', 'what the AC outlets can carry'), the picks change. (1) The Anker Nano 67 W is effectively a 45 W laptop charger in normal desk use. A shopper who needs the full 65 W while also charging a phone should look at the Anker Prime 140 W (A9128), which already sits in our table. (2) The Anker 351's 20 W USB-C is really a 'USB-C alone' figure. (3) TESSAN's own PS07 listing puts the 8 outlets at 1,250 W max, against 1,875 W on the Anker 351 and Nano. That rules the PS07 out for a space heater, a hair dryer, or a 1,500 W kettle plus a laptop. (4) Every candidate's surge figure is a joule number the maker declares with no UL 1449 VPR, so joules shouldn't decide between them. Our table should change 'Surge' to 'Surge (maker-declared J; no VPR stated)' and add an 'AC max' column.

findings.label: USB-C output by port combination
findings.value: 67 W from one USB-C alone; 45 W + 12 W with USB-C + USB-A; 20 W + 45 W with two USB-C; 20 W + 30 W + 12 W with 2× USB-C + USB-A; 20 W + 30 W + 15 W (USB-A shared) with all four
findings.source_title: Anker Nano Charging Station (6-in-1, 67W) – Anker US
findings.note: Taken from Anker's multi-port output table. A laptop on the best USB-C port drops from 67 W to 45 W as soon as any second USB device is connected. The page lists certifications as TUV, FCC, CP65, ICES and PSE, with no joule rating and no UL 1449. The product showed as Sold Out on anker.com with no price.

findings.label: AC rating / cord
findings.value: 125 V, 15 A, 1,875 W; 2 AC outlets; 5 ft (1.5 m) cord
findings.source_title: Anker Nano Charging Station (6-in-1, 67W) – Anker US
findings.note: This rating covers the whole unit; Anker gives no per-outlet figure.

findings.label: USB-C condition
findings.value: 20 W (5 V 3 A / 9 V 2.22 A / 12 V 1.67 A) only when both USB-A ports are unused
findings.source_title: Anker 351 Power Strip (12 Outlets) – Anker US
findings.note: Anker's wording: '20W USB-C charging is only available when the 2 USB-A ports are not in use.' The page does not give the USB-C level when USB-A is in use. USB-A is 2.4 A max per port.

findings.label: AC max load / surge / certification / price
findings.source_title: Anker 351 Power Strip (12 Outlets) – Anker US
findings.note: The 2,100 J figure appears only in image alt text, not in the spec table. No UL 1449 listing or VPR/clamping voltage is given. $28.99 is the Black variant on anker.com, the same price as ChatGPT's Walmart card.

findings.label: AC max load
findings.value: 1,250 W max across the 8 AC outlets
findings.source_title: TESSAN 20W Surge Protector Power Strip PS07
findings.note: TESSAN's copy reads '8 AC outlets (up to 1250W)'. The second PS07 listing (https://www.tessan.com/products/flat-extension-cord-surge-protector-power-strip-ps07, $29.99) also says '8 AC outlets (1250W Max)'. That is 1,250 W against 1,875 W on the Anker 351 and Nano, about 10.4 A against 15 A at 120 V. I read both listings through storecheck.py's Shopify product data. A direct page fetch returned HTTP 429.

findings.label: USB-C wording / price
findings.value: 'USB C2 delivers to PD 20W max'; USB-A 12 W max per port; $28.99 (surge-protector-power-strip-ps07) / $29.99 (flat-extension-cord listing)
findings.source_title: TESSAN Flat Extension Cord Surge Protector Power Strip
findings.note: TESSAN names only port 'C2' as 20 W PD. Our current table says '20 W PD each', which this copy doesn't support, so the row should change to '20 W PD on C2' until a manual says otherwise. The $28.99 listing's headline also says '2000J' while its body says '2100J'. No UL/ETL or VPR is stated in either listing.

findings.label: Surge rating comparability
findings.value: None of the candidate maker pages I read (Anker A9192, A9129, TESSAN PS07) states a UL 1449 listing or a VPR/clamping voltage; joules are each maker's own claim
findings.source_title: Best Power Strips (2026): 7 Picks Compared for Home and Desk - InspectandTest
findings.note: InspectandTest says none of the 18 listings it reviewed states a clamping voltage ('often printed as VPR') and calls joule figures self-reported. I confirmed on the maker pages above that the same is true for these three candidates.

findings.label: What rivals already say on USB sharing
findings.value: rottenwifi: Anker 351 USB-C 20 W only with USB-A idle; CyberPower P405UC 18 W total. itechguides: Nano Clamp '70W total, not 70W independently from every port'
findings.source_title: Best USB Surge Protectors in 2026: Anker and CyberPower Picks
findings.note: I also read https://www.itechguides.com/best-usb-power-strips-in-2026-top-picks-for-desks-laptops-and-home-offices/ on 2026-11-17. Neither page covers the A9129 67 W→45 W split or the TESSAN 1,250 W AC limit.
